analysis.one_liner: Cuts the Social Security payroll tax for workers and employers, ending the stockpiling of the trust fund surplus.
analysis.headline: A 54-44 majority of senators voted to let the bill proceed, but that fell short of the 60 votes needed to waive a budget rule, so the bill was ruled out of order and never got a vote on its merits.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the early 1980s, Social Security taxes have been set deliberately high so the program collects more than it pays out, building a surplus in its trust fund. This bill, sponsored by Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, would have cut the Social Security payroll tax for both workers and employers — from 6.2% down to 5.1% for each through most of the 1990s and 2000s — while sharply raising the wage ceiling so higher earners paid more, and scheduling higher taxes starting in 2020 to cover the baby-boom retirement wave. The idea was to stop collecting a surplus that was, in practice, being lent to the federal government to make the overall deficit look smaller.
analysis.who_benefits: Every worker who pays Social Security taxes would see the rate cut immediately, with the employee share dropping from 6.2% to 5.1% by 1996; the self-employed rate would fall from 12.4% to 10.2%. Employers would get an identical cut in the share they pay. Higher earners would pay more, because the bill raises the maximum wage subject to the tax from $51,300 to $85,500 by 1996.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the employee and employer Social Security tax rate from 6.2% to 5.1% from 1996 through 2009, and cuts the self-employment rate from 12.4% to 10.2%, putting money back in every working paycheck.
The Congressional Research Service summary describes the bill as providing reduced Social Security tax rates until 2015, with the increases not beginning until 2020.
The bill raises the maximum wage subject to Social Security tax on a graduated schedule, from $51,300 in 1990 to $85,500 by 1996, shifting more of the burden onto higher earners.
The bill's stated purpose is to return Social Security to pay-as-you-go financing, so current taxes cover current benefits instead of accumulating a surplus.
The bill also reallocates a growing share of revenue to the Disability Insurance trust fund over time.

analysis.who_pays: The Social Security trust fund would collect far less during the 1990s and 2000s, giving up the surplus buildup that was scheduled ahead of the baby-boom retirements of the 2010s and 2020s. Future workers would face scheduled tax increases starting in 2020, climbing to 8.1% by 2055 — well above today's 6.2%. The federal government would lose the surplus that makes the overall budget deficit look smaller on paper.
analysis.who_pays_short: The trust fund and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill schedules higher Social Security tax rates beginning in 2020, rising to 8.1% for employees and employers by 2055 — meaning the cut for today's workers is paid for by higher taxes on future workers, just as the baby-boom generation retires.

Cutting rates through 2009 abandons the trust fund buildup during precisely the years Social Security was designed to stockpile reserves ahead of boomer retirements; critics argued that a pay-as-you-go program with no cushion is far more exposed to economic downturns and demographic surprises.
The employer share is cut on the same schedule as the employee share, so roughly half of the tax reduction flows to employers rather than to workers' take-home pay.
The bill was killed on a budget-rule point of order, not on its merits — no senator ever got an up-or-down vote on whether the tax cut itself was wise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate gain is real and broad: a payroll tax cut for every working American at a time when the trust fund was taking in more than it needed. But the trade-off is genuine, and an honest supporter had to concede it — the bill gives up roughly two decades of surplus accumulation ahead of the largest retirement wave in American history, and buys that back with scheduled tax increases on workers in the 2020s and beyond. Whether that was prudent depended on whether you believed the surplus was safe in the trust fund or was effectively being spent by the general government. The bill never got the floor debate that question deserved.

outcome.mechanism: A senator raised a budget-rule objection; 54 senators voted to set the rule aside, but 60 votes were required, so the presiding officer ruled the bill out of order and it went back to the calendar, where it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan introduced the bill on October 5, 1990, and it was placed on the Senate calendar without any committee stops.

On October 10, 1990, the Senate took it up by unanimous consent, but a point of order was raised that the bill violated section 311 of the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 — a budget rule covering this kind of tax legislation.
Overcoming that objection required 60 votes; the motion to waive the Budget Act failed 54-44, with 42 of 55 Democrats voting to proceed but only 12 of 45 Republicans.
With the waiver failed, the chair ruled the bill out of order, two pending amendments fell with it, and the bill was returned to the calendar.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill never received a vote on its merits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the Social Security surplus kept building up in the trust fund — money the federal government could borrow to make the overall deficit look smaller — and higher earners avoided the bill's sharply higher wage cap. Workers kept paying the full 6.2% payroll tax on every dollar of wages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The deficit-accounting status quo and high earners

for.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it straight to the Senate floor within days, arguing Social Security taxes had been raised too high and the surplus was masking the deficit.

for.name: 42 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate Democrats voting to waive the budget rule
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the motion to waive the Budget Act, which would have let the bill receive a vote.

for.name: 12 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.role: Senate Republicans voting to waive the budget rule
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the motion to waive the Budget Act.

against.name: 31 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate Republicans voting against waiving the budget rule
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to waive the Budget Act, dooming the bill to a ruling of order.

against.name: 13 of 55 Senate Democrats
against.role: Senate Democrats voting against waiving the budget rule
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to waive the Budget Act.

against.name: The presiding officer of the Senate
against.role: Chair enforcing the Budget Act point of order
against.what_they_did: After the waiver vote failed, ruled the bill out of order and returned it to the calendar, killing its pending amendments.

against.name: President George H. W. Bush and his administration
against.role: White House, during the 1990 budget negotiations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Moynihan's plan during the fall 1990 budget fight, warning that cutting Social Security taxes would drain the trust fund at a time of large deficits.

sides.party_line_note: The vote to let the bill proceed was 54-44, but it split sharply by party: 42 of 55 Democrats voted yes while only 12 of 45 Republicans did, and the 60-vote threshold meant the Republican bloc alone was enough to kill it.

industries.note: The bill cuts the employer share of the Social Security tax on the same schedule as the employee share, from 6.2% to 5.1%, lowering the cost of every payroll dollar. Workers get the same rate cut, so the two interests move together here — though economists often note that the employer share eventually shows up in wages either way.

industries.industry: High-income earners above the wage cap
industries.note: The bill raises the maximum wage subject to Social Security tax from $51,300 to $85,500 by 1996, so high earners would have paid substantially more even as their marginal rate fell. Their interest ran against the bill.
